stem: A 22-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to acute vision disturbances and headache.  About an hour ago, the patient experienced a small area of vision loss, which she describes as "a hole in her vision."  The vision disturbance gradually expanded to a C shape in her peripheral visual field and spontaneously resolved after 15-20 minutes.  A progressively worsening, severe, right-sided headache of pulsating quality quickly followed.  The patient has had similar headaches but not of such severity.  She has no other medical conditions and takes no medications.  Blood pressure is 150/86 mm Hg and pulse is 92/min.  On physical examination, the patient is lying still in bed with her eyes closed.  The pupils are equal and reactive to light.  Funduscopic examination reveals no abnormalities.  Bilateral upper and lower extremity muscle strength, deep tendon reflexes, and sensation are normal.  Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌​​​‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌​​‌​​​​​​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​​​​​‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​
explanation:
This young woman with a pulsating unilateral headache preceded by visual field loss has migraine with aura.  Migraine is an episodic neurologic disorder that results in severe, unilateral, throbbing headaches often associated with photophobia, phonophobia, and nausea/vomiting.  Migraines typically last 4-72 hours.  The condition has a strong genetic predisposition, and women are affected more frequently than men.

Migraines are accompanied by focal, reversible neurologic symptoms, known as auras, in about 25% of patients.  Migraines seem to start with a self-propagating wave of depolarization spreading across the cerebral cortex that is sometimes followed by a period of brief neuronal suppression.  This cortical depolarization/suppression is thought to be what causes both positive neurologic symptoms (eg, bright spots, noises, paresthesia) and negative neurologic symptoms (eg, vision defects, hearing loss, numbness).  Auras develop progressively over minutes and last less than an hour.  The depolarization eventually spreads to trigeminal nerve nociceptors, which causes severe headache to develop, usually after an aura resolves.

(Choice A)  Acute angle-closure glaucoma causes headache and decreased vision associated with elevated intraocular pressures.  However, patients are typically older (age >60), and severe eye pain and conjunctival erythema are common.  Vision would not be expected to improve without intervention.

(Choice B)  Cluster headache causes severe unilateral headaches; ipsilateral autonomic symptoms (eg, lacrimation, rhinorrhea, flushing, diaphoresis) are expected.  In contrast to migraine, cluster headache is not associated with aura; it is also more common in men.

(Choice C)  A focal seizure may be preceded by an aura, but seizures typically cause positive symptoms (eg, lip smacking, arm movement, seeing bright lights) rather than the negative symptoms this patient experienced.  In addition, seizures typically last <2 minutes and unilateral headache is more suggestive of migraine with aura.

(Choice E)  Optic neuritis is a demyelinating disorder that causes unilateral vision loss that typically progresses over a period of weeks.  Other features of optic neuritis include eye pain that is worse with movement, changes in color vision, and an afferent pupillary defect.

(Choice F)  Transient ischemic attacks (TIAs) cause focal neurologic deficits, but they typically have an acute onset with maximal symptoms at onset rather than the progressive visual field defect this patient experienced.  In addition, TIAs usually occur in older patients with vascular risk factors (eg, smoking, hyperlipidemia) and would be very uncommon in an otherwise healthy young woman; this patient's elevated blood pressure is most likely secondary to pain from acute migraine.

Educational objective:Migraine is an episodic neurologic disorder that results in severe, unilateral, throbbing headaches that are often associated with photophobia, phonophobia, and nausea/vomiting.  Migraine attacks typically last 4-72 hours, and up to 25% of patients also develop an aura (focal, reversible neurologic symptoms that precede or accompany the headache).​‌​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌​‌‌‌​​‌​​​‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌‌‌‌​‌‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌​​​‌​​​​‌​​​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​​‌‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​​‌​‌​​​‌​‌‌​​​‌​‌‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​‌​​​​‌​‌‌​​‌​​​​‌‌​‌‌‌‌‌‌​​​​‌​‌‌​‌​‌​​​‌​‌​‌‌‌​‌​‌​‌​‌​​‌​​‌​​‌‌​​‌‌‌​​​​​​​‌​​‌​​​​​​​​‌‌​​​‌​‌​​​​​​​‌​​‌​​‌​​​‌​‌​​‌‌‌​​​‌‌​​​‌‌​‌‌‌​​​‌​‌​​‌​‌‌‌‌​​‌‌‌‌‌‌​‌‌​​‌​‌​​​​‌​​‌‌​‌​
